{{Short description|Concept in logic}}
A '''substitution''' is a [[syntax (logic)|syntactic]] transformation on [[formal language|formal]] expressions.
To ''apply'' a substitution to an [[Expression (mathematics)|expression]] means to consistently replace its variable, or placeholder, symbols with other expressions.{{citation needed|date=September 2025}}

The resulting expression is called a ''substitution instance'', or  ''instance'' for short, of the original expression.

== Propositional logic ==
=== Definition ===
Where ''ψ'' and ''φ'' represent [[Well-formed formula|formula]]s of [[propositional logic]], ''ψ'' is a ''substitution instance'' of ''φ'' [[if and only if]] ''ψ'' may be obtained from ''φ'' by substituting formulas for [[propositional variable]]s in ''φ'', replacing each occurrence of the same variable by an occurrence of the same formula. For example:

::''ψ:'' (R → S) & (T → S)
is a substitution instance of
::''φ:'' P & Q
That is, ''ψ'' can be obtained by replacing P and Q in ''φ'' with (R → S) and (T → S) respectively. Similarly:
::''ψ:'' (A ↔ A) ↔ (A ↔ A)
is a substitution instance of:
::''φ:'' (A ↔ A)

since ''ψ'' can be obtained by replacing each A in ''φ'' with (A ↔ A).

In some [[deduction system]]s for propositional logic, a new expression (a [[proposition]]) may be entered on a line of a derivation if it is a substitution instance of a previous line of the derivation.<ref>{{Hunter 1996|p=118}}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=December 2024}} This is how new lines are introduced in some [[axiomatic system]]s. In systems that use [[rule of inference|rules of transformation]], a rule may include the use of a ''substitution instance'' for the purpose of introducing certain variables into a derivation.

=== Tautologies ===
A propositional formula is a [[tautology (logic)|tautology]] if it is true under every [[valuation (logic)|valuation]] (or [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretation]]) of its predicate symbols. If Φ is a tautology, and Θ is a substitution instance of Φ, then Θ is again a tautology. This fact implies the soundness of the deduction rule described in the previous section.

== First-order logic ==

In [[first-order logic]], a ''substitution'' is a total mapping  {{math|''σ'': ''V'' → ''T''}} from [[term (logic)#Formal definition|variables]] to [[Term (logic)|terms]]; many,<ref name="Duffy.1991"/>{{rp|73}}<ref name="Baader.Snyder.2001"/>{{rp|445}} but not all<ref name="Dershowitz.Jouannaud.1990">{{cite book | author1=N. Dershowitz |author2= J.-P. Jouannaud | contribution=Rewrite Systems | pages=243–320 | editor=[[Jan van Leeuwen]] | title=Formal Models and Semantics | publisher=Elsevier | series=Handbook of Theoretical Computer Science | volume=B | year=1990}}</ref>{{rp|250}} authors additionally require ''σ''(''x'') = ''x'' for all but finitely many variables ''x''. The notation {{mset| ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''x''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>''k''</sub> }}<ref group=note>Some authors use [ ''t''<sub>1</sub>/''x''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''t''<sub>''k''</sub>/''x''<sub>''k''</sub> ] to denote that substitution, e.g. {{cite book| author=M. Wirsing| title=Algebraic Specification| year=1990| volume=B| pages=675–788| publisher=Elsevier| editor=Jan van Leeuwen| series=Handbook of Theoretical Computer Science}}, here: p. 682.</ref>
refers to a substitution mapping each variable ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> to the corresponding term ''t''<sub>''i''</sub>, for ''i''=1,…,''k'', and every other variable to itself; the ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> must be pairwise distinct. Most authors additionally require each term ''t''<sub>''i''</sub> to be syntactically different from ''x''<sub>''i''</sub>, to avoid infinitely many distinct notations for the same substitution. ''Applying'' that substitution to a term ''t'' is written in [[postfix notation]] as ''t'' {{mset| ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''x''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>''k''</sub> }}; it means to (simultaneously) replace every occurrence of each ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> in ''t'' by ''t''<sub>''i''</sub>.<ref group=note>From a [[term algebra]] point of view, the set ''T'' of terms is the [[Free object#Definition|free term algebra]] over the set ''V'' of variables, hence for each substitution mapping σ: ''V'' → ''T'' there is a unique [[Universal algebra#Basic constructions|homomorphism]] {{overline|σ}}: ''T'' → ''T'' that agrees with σ on ''V'' ⊆ ''T''; the above-defined application of ''σ'' to a term ''t'' is then viewed as applying the function {{overline|''σ''}} to the argument ''t''.</ref> The result ''tσ'' of applying a substitution ''σ'' to a term ''t'' is called an ''instance'' of that term ''t''.
For example, applying the substitution {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'', ''z''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''h''(''a'',''y'') }} to the term 
:{|
|-
|| ''f''(
| style="text-align: center;" |''z''
||, ''a'', ''g''(
|| ''x''
|| ), ''y'') &nbsp; 
|| yields 
|-
|| ''f''(
|| ''h''(''a'',''y'')
||, ''a'', ''g''(
|| ''z''
|| ), ''y'')
|| .
|}

The ''domain'' ''dom''(''σ'') of a substitution ''σ'' is commonly defined as the set of variables actually replaced, i.e. ''dom''(''σ'') = {{mset| ''x'' ∈ ''V'' | ''xσ'' ≠ ''x'' }}.
A substitution is called a ''ground'' substitution if it maps all variables of its domain to [[term (logic)#Ground and linear terms|ground]], i.e. variable-free, terms.
The substitution instance ''tσ'' of a ground substitution is a ground term if all of ''t''{{'}}s variables are in ''σ''{{'}}s domain, i.e. if ''vars''(''t'') ⊆ ''dom''(''σ'').
A substitution ''σ'' is called a ''linear'' substitution if ''tσ'' is a [[term (logic)#Ground and linear terms|linear]] term for some (and hence every) linear term ''t'' containing precisely the variables of ''σ''{{'}}s domain, i.e. with ''vars''(''t'') = ''dom''(''σ'').
A substitution ''σ'' is called a ''flat'' substitution if ''xσ'' is a variable for every variable ''x''.
A substitution ''σ'' is called a ''renaming'' substitution if it is a [[Permutation#Permutations in group theory|permutation]] on the set of all variables. Like every permutation, a renaming substitution σ always has an ''inverse'' substitution ''σ''<sup>−1</sup>, such that ''tσσ''<sup>−1</sup> = ''t'' = ''tσ''<sup>−1</sup>''σ'' for every term ''t''. However, it is not possible to define an inverse for an arbitrary substitution.

For example, {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;2, ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;3+4 }} is a ground substitution, {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>+4 }} is non-ground and non-flat, but linear,
{{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>+4 }} is non-linear and non-flat, {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub> }} is flat, but non-linear, {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub> }} is both linear and flat, but not a renaming, since it maps both ''y'' and ''y''<sub>2</sub> to ''y''<sub>2</sub>; each of these substitutions has the set {{mset|''x'',''y''}} as its domain. An example for a renaming substitution is {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y'', ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''x'' }}, it has the inverse {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y'', ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''x'' }}. The flat substitution {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'', ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'' }} cannot have an inverse, since e.g. (''x''+''y'') {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'', ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'' }} = ''z''+''z'', and the latter term cannot be transformed back to ''x''+''y'', as the information about the origin a ''z'' stems from is lost. The ground substitution {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;2 }} cannot have an inverse due to a similar loss of origin information e.g. in (''x''+2) {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;2 }} = 2+2, even if replacing constants by variables was allowed by some fictitious kind of "generalized substitutions".

Two substitutions are considered ''equal'' if they map each variable to [[Term (logic)#Structural equality|syntactically equal]] result terms, formally: ''σ'' = ''τ'' if ''xσ'' = ''xτ'' for each variable ''x'' ∈ ''V''.
The ''composition'' of two substitutions ''σ'' = {{mset| ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''x''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>''k''</sub> }} and ''τ'' = {{mset| ''y''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''u''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''y''<sub>''l''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;u<sub>''l''</sub> }} is obtained by removing from the substitution {{mset| ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>1</sub>''τ'', …, ''x''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>''k''</sub>''τ'',  ''y''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''u''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''y''<sub>''l''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''u''<sub>''l''</sub> }} those pairs ''y''<sub>''i''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''u''<sub>''i''</sub> for which ''y''<sub>''i''</sub> ∈ {{mset| ''x''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''x''<sub>''k''</sub> }}.
The composition of ''σ'' and ''τ'' is denoted by ''στ''. Composition is an [[associative operation]], and is compatible with substitution application, i.e. (''ρσ'')''τ'' = ''ρ''(''στ''), and (''tσ'')''τ'' = ''t''(''στ''), respectively, for every substitutions ''ρ'', ''σ'', ''τ'', and every term ''t''.
The ''identity substitution'', which maps every variable to itself, is the [[neutral element]] of substitution composition. A substitution ''σ'' is called ''idempotent'' if ''σσ'' = ''σ'', and hence ''tσσ'' = ''tσ'' for every term ''t''. When ''x''<sub>''i''</sub>≠''t''<sub>''i''</sub> for all ''i'', the substitution {{mset| ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''x''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''t''<sub>''k''</sub> }} is idempotent if and only if none of the variables ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> occurs in any ''t''<sub>''j''</sub>. Substitution composition is not commutative, that is, ''στ'' may be different from ''τσ'', even if ''σ'' and ''τ'' are idempotent.<ref name="Duffy.1991">{{cite book| author=David A. Duffy| title=Principles of Automated Theorem Proving| year=1991| publisher=Wiley}}</ref>{{rp|73–74}}<ref name="Baader.Snyder.2001">{{cite book| author=[[Franz Baader]], [[Wayne Snyder]]| title=Unification Theory| year=2001| pages=439–526| publisher=Elsevier| editor=[[John Alan Robinson|Alan Robinson]] and [[Andrei Voronkov (computer scientist)|Andrei Voronkov]]| url=http://www.cs.bu.edu/~snyder/publications/UnifChapter.pdf| access-date=2014-09-24| archive-date=2015-06-08| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150608053650/http://www.cs.bu.edu/~snyder/publications/UnifChapter.pdf| url-status=dead}}</ref>{{rp|445–446}}

For example, {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;2, ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;3+4 }} is equal to {{mset| ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;3+4, ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;2 }}, but different from {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;2, ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;7 }}. The substitution {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''+''y'' }} is idempotent, e.g. ((''x''+''y'') {{mset|''x''↦''y''+''y''}}) {{mset|''x''↦''y''+''y''}} = ((''y''+''y'')+''y'') {{mset|''x''↦''y''+''y''}} = (''y''+''y'')+''y'', while the substitution {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''x''+''y'' }} is non-idempotent, e.g. ((''x''+''y'') {{mset|''x''↦''x''+''y''}}) {{mset|''x''↦''x''+''y''}} = ((''x''+''y'')+''y'') {{mset|''x''↦''x''+''y''}} = ((''x''+''y'')+''y'')+''y''. An example for non-commuting substitutions is {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y'' }} {{mset| ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'' }} = {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'', ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'' }}, but {{mset| ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z''}} {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y''}} = {{mset| ''x''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''y'', ''y''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;''z'' }}.

==Mathematics==
In [[mathematics]], there are two common uses of substitution: ''substitution of [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]]'' for [[Constant (mathematics)|constants]] (also called [[Assignment (computer science)|assignment]] for that variable), and the ''substitution property of [[Equality (mathematics)|equality]]'',<ref>{{SpringerEOM|title=Equality axioms|oldid=46837|last=Sobolev|first=S. K.}}</ref> also called [[Identity_of_indiscernibles|''Leibniz's Law'']].<ref>Deutsch, Harry and Pawel Garbacz, "Relative Identity", The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Fall 2024 Edition), Edward N. Zalta & Uri Nodelman (eds.), forthcoming URL: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/identity-relative/#StanAccoIden</ref>

Considering mathematics as a [[formal language]], a variable is a [[Symbol (mathematics)|symbol]] from an [[Alphabet (formal languages)|alphabet]], usually a letter like {{Mvar|x}}, {{Mvar|y}}, and {{Mvar|z}}, which denotes a range of possible [[Value (mathematics)|values]].<ref name=":0">{{SpringerEOM|title=Individual variable|oldid=17515|last=Sobolev|first=S. K.}}</ref> If a variable is [[Free variables and bound variables|free]] in a given [[Expression (mathematics)|expression]] or [[Formula#In mathematics|formula]], then it can be replaced with any of the values in its range.<ref>{{SpringerEOM|title=Free variable|oldid=46988|last=Sobolev|first=S. K.}}</ref> Certain kinds of bound variables can be substituted too. For instance, [[parameter]]s of an expression (like the [[coefficient]]s of a [[polynomial]]), or the [[Argument of a function|argument]] of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]]. Moreover, variables being [[universally quantified]] can be replaced with any of the values in its range, and the result will a true [[Statement (logic)|statement]]. (This is called [[Universal instantiation]])

For a non-formalized language, that is, in most mathematical texts outside of [[mathematical logic]], for an individual expression it is not always possible to identify which variables are free and bound. For example, in <math display="inline">\sum_{i < k} a_{ik}</math>, depending on the context, the variable <math display="inline">i</math> can be free and <math display="inline">k</math> bound, or vice-versa, but they cannot both be free. Determining which value is assumed to be free depends on context and [[Semantics of logic|semantics]].

The ''substitution property of equality'', or ''Leibniz's Law'' (though the latter term is usually reserved for [[philosophical]] contexts), generally states that, if two things are equal, then any property of one, must be a property of the other. It can be formally stated in [[Logic notation|logical notation]] as:<math display="block">(a=b) \implies \bigl[ \phi(a) \Rightarrow \phi(b) \bigr] </math>For every <math display="inline">a </math> and <math display="inline">b </math>, and any [[well-formed formula]] <math display="inline">\phi(x) </math> (with a free variable x). For example: For all [[real numbers]] {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}}, if {{math|1=''a'' = ''b''}}, then {{math|''a'' ≥ 0}} implies {{math|''b'' ≥ 0}} (here, <math>\phi(x)</math> is {{math|''x'' ≥ 0}}). This is a property which is most often used in [[algebra]], especially in solving [[System of equations|systems of equations]], but is applied in nearly every area of math that uses equality. This, taken together with the [[reflexive property]] of equality, forms the [[First-order logic#Equality and its axioms|axioms of equality]] in first-order logic.<ref>[[Melvin Fitting|Fitting, M.]], ''First-Order Logic and Automated Theorem Proving'' (Berlin/Heidelberg: Springer, 1990), [https://books.google.com/books?id=eaXbBwAAQBAJ&pg=PT198 pp. 198–200].</ref>

Substitution is related to, but not identical to, [[function composition]]; it is closely related to ''β''-reduction in [[lambda calculus]]. In contrast to these notions, however, the accent in algebra is on the preservation of algebraic structure by the substitution operation, the fact that substitution gives a [[homomorphism]] for the structure at hand (in the case of polynomials, the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] structure).{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

=== {{Visible anchor|Algebra}} ===
Substitution is a basic operation in [[algebra]], in particular in [[computer algebra]].<ref name="HoftHoft2002">{{cite book|author1=Margret H. Hoft|author2=Hartmut F.W. Hoft|title=Computing with Mathematica|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5bQRX0w0gtAC&q=substitution|date=6 November 2002|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-08-048855-4}}</ref><ref name="HECK2012">{{cite book|author=Andre Heck|title=Introduction to Maple|url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoma0000heck|url-access=registration|quote=substitution.|date=6 December 2012|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4684-0484-5}}</ref>

A common case of substitution involves [[polynomial]]s, where substitution of a numerical value (or another expression) for the indeterminate of a univariate polynomial amounts to evaluating the polynomial at that value. Indeed, this operation occurs so frequently that the notation for polynomials is often adapted to it; instead of designating a polynomial by a name like ''P'', as one would do for other mathematical objects, one could define
:<math>P(X)=X^5-3X^2+5X-17</math>
so that substitution for ''X'' can be designated by replacement inside "''P''(''X'')", say
:<math>P(2) = 13</math>
or
:<math>P(X+1) = X^5 + 5X^4 + 10X^3 + 7X^2 + 4X - 14.</math>
Substitution can also be applied to other kinds of formal objects built from symbols, for instance elements of [[free group]]s. In order for substitution to be defined, one needs an algebraic structure with an appropriate [[universal property]], that asserts the existence of unique homomorphisms that send indeterminates to specific values; the substitution then amounts to finding the image of an element under such a homomorphism.

=== Proof of substitution in ZFC ===
The following is a proof of the substitution property of equality in ZFC (as defined in first-order logic without equality), which is adapted from ''Introduction to Axiomatic Set Theory'' (1982) by Gaisi Takeuti and Wilson M. Zaring.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Takeuti |first=Gaisi |last2=Zaring |first2=Wilson M. |date=1982 |title=Introduction to Axiomatic Set Theory |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4613-8168-6 |journal=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |language=en |pages=6-9 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-8168-6 |issn=0072-5285 |archive-url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoax00take/page/8/ |archive-date=2014-08-06|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 
{{Math theorem|if <math>a = b</math>, then, for any well-formed formula <math>\phi</math>, <math>\phi(a) \Rightarrow \phi(b)</math>.}}

See [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory#Formal language|Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory § Formal language]] for the definition of formulas in ZFC. The [[Recursive definition|definition is recursive]], so a proof by [[Mathematical induction|induction]] is used. In ZFC in first-order logic without equality, "set equality" is defined to mean that two sets have the same elements, written symbolically as "for all z, z is in x if and only if z is in y". Then, the Axiom of Extensionality asserts that if two sets have the same elements, then they belong to the same sets:

{{math theorem|name=Definition|<math display="block">(x=y) := \forall z [z \in x \Leftrightarrow z \in y] </math>}}

{{math theorem|name=Axiom|<math display="block">(x = y) \Rightarrow \forall z (x \in z \Leftrightarrow y \in z)  </math>}}

{{math proof|title=Base formulas
|
Let <math>X, Y, Z</math>, be metavariables for any variables or sets, such that <math>X = Y</math>

Case 1: <math>\phi(X): (Z \in X)</math>
<blockquote>Assume <math>Z \in X</math>, then, by the definition of equality, <math>Z \in Y</math>, thus <math>(X=Y) \implies \bigl[ Z \in X \Rightarrow Z \in Y \bigr]   </math></blockquote>
Case 2: <math>\phi(X): (X \in Z )</math>
<blockquote>Assume <math>X \in Z</math>, then by the axiom of extensionality, <math>Y \in Z </math>, thus <math>(X=Y) \implies \bigl[ X \in Z \Rightarrow Y \in Z \bigr]   </math></blockquote>
}}

{{math proof|title=Recursive formulas
|
Let <math>\psi, \varphi</math> be meta variables for any formulas with the property that <math>(a=b) \implies \bigl[ \phi(a) \Rightarrow \phi(b) \bigr] </math>. Let <math>X, Y</math>, be metavariables for any variables or sets, such that <math>X = Y</math>, and let <math>z</math> be a metavariable for any variable.

Case 1: <math>\neg (\psi)</math>
<blockquote>Since <math>X = Y</math>, then <math>Y= X</math> by symmetry of equality, therefore <math>\bigl[ \psi(Y) \Rightarrow \psi(X) \bigr] </math>, by the induction hypothesis, therefore <math>\bigl[ \neg\psi(X) \Rightarrow  \neg\psi(Y) \bigr] </math> by [[contraposition]], thus <math>(X=Y) \implies \bigl[ \neg\psi(X) \Rightarrow  \neg\psi(Y) \bigr]</math></blockquote>
Case 2: <math>\psi \land \varphi</math>
<blockquote>Since <math>X=Y</math>, then <math>\bigl[ \psi(X) \Rightarrow \psi(Y) \bigr] </math> and <math>\bigl[ \varphi(X) \Rightarrow \varphi(Y) \bigr] </math>, which implies <math>\bigl[ \bigl( \psi(X) \land \varphi(X)\bigr) \Rightarrow \psi(Y) \land \varphi(Y) \bigr) \bigr] </math>, thus <math>(X=Y) \implies \bigl[ \bigl( \psi(X) \land \varphi(X)\bigr) \Rightarrow \psi(Y) \land \varphi(Y) \bigr) \bigr] </math></blockquote>
Case 3: <math>\exists z(\psi)</math>
<blockquote>Since <math>X=Y</math>,  <math>\psi(X, z) \Rightarrow \psi(Y, z)  </math> assume by [[Proof by contradiction|way of contradiction]] that the result is false, that is <math>\exists z(\psi(X,z))  </math> is true but <math>\exists z(\psi(Y,z))  </math> is false. By [[existential instantiation]], let <math>z_0</math> denote the value such that <math>\psi(X, z_0)   </math> is true. Then <math>\psi(Y,z_0)    </math> is false by asumption, and therefore  <math>\psi(X, z_0) \Rightarrow \psi(Y, z_0)   </math> is false, which contradicts our induction hypothesis, and the result follows.</blockquote>
}}
